title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In managed care, distribution is easy to buy with rich benefits; the real moat is pricing discipline at the point of renewal and claims settlement.
epigraph.author: Actuarial Underwriting Maxim

web_blocks.html: UnitedHealth Group's go-to-market machine runs across three main distribution channels [1, 19]. First, B2B employer and consultant networks—including Mercer, Aon, Willis Towers Watson, and regional brokers—distribute Commercial ASO and risk-based plans [1, 19]. Second, direct-to-senior and broker-assisted enrollment drives Medicare Advantage and Supplement sign-ups during the CMS Annual Election Period (Oct 15–Dec 7), backed by AARP co-branding [1, 19]. Third, multi-year state RFP bidding wins Medicaid Community & State contracts [1, 19]. On the Optum side, Optum Insight and Optum Rx deploy enterprise sales teams targeting health systems, state governments, and competing regional Blue Cross plans.

web_blocks.title: Supply Chain & Network Mechanics: How the Claim Dollar Moves

web_blocks.html: Unlike a manufacturing firm, UNH's 'supply chain' consists of contracted hospital systems, independent physician practices, drugmakers, and pharmacy networks. UnitedHealthcare contracts with over 1.7 million physicians and care professionals and 6,000+ hospitals [1]. It uses local market density to negotiate unit-price discounts off hospital chargemaster rates [1]. In 2025–2026, following intense provider and regulatory pushback, UNH overhauled its utilization-management friction [7, 15]. Management pledged to cut prior-authorization volume by 30% by year-end 2026 [7, 15]. It also cut pediatric prior authorizations by nearly two-thirds and sped up payments to 1,500 rural hospitals [7, 15].

On the pharmacy supply chain, Optum Rx aggregates volume across 1.6 billion annual adjusted prescriptions [7, 20]. That scale helps negotiate rebates from drugmakers and dispensing fees from 65,000+ retail pharmacies [7, 20]. Meanwhile, Optum routes high-margin specialty biologics and biosimilars through its own specialty and home-delivery pharmacies [7, 20]. Importantly, Optum Rx is moving clients to a transparent per-member fee model with 100% manufacturer rebate pass-through by January 1, 2028 [7].

Even so, negative working capital (claims float) and sub-1% CapEx intensity converted that into $3.59 of Free Cash Flow.

web_blocks.title: Value-Based Care Economics: Why Optum Health Swung in 2025–2026

web_blocks.html: A critical nuance in UNH's unit economics is the split between fee-for-service (FFS) care and fully accountable value-based care (VBC) inside Optum Health [9, 13]. In FFS clinics, Optum earns a margin per visit or procedure. In VBC, Optum Health accepts a global capitated budget—roughly 80%–85% of the CMS premium—to cover all medical costs for ~4.3–5.0 million high-acuity seniors [9]. In 2025, CMS phased in the V28 risk-adjustment model, which stripped out certain chronic-condition diagnosis weights [5]. Hospital and outpatient utilization jumped at the same time [5]. Optum Health's fixed clinical overhead could not absorb the medical-cost overrun. As a result, the segment swung from $7.77 billion in 2024 operating earnings to a $(278) million loss in 2025 [5]. In 2026, UNH exited ~700,000 VBC patients in under-scaled markets and renegotiated legacy third-party payer contracts [7, 9]. Those steps restored Optum Health's operating margin to 4.3% in 9M 2026, or $3.07 billion in EBIT [7, 9].

web_blocks.title: Why Insurance Float & Days Claims Payable Matter
paragraphs: UnitedHealthcare collects premiums upfront at the start of each month and pays hospital and physician claims 45–50 days later [7]. Days Claims Payable stood at 47.0 days in Q3 2026, with $39.35 billion in medical costs payable on the balance sheet [7]. That structural float sits alongside $86.6 billion in cash and investment securities [7]. Together, they generated $3.92 billion in investment and other income in FY2025 [2] and $3.43 billion in 9M 2026 [7].

web_blocks.title: Hidden Unit-Economics Frictions: Reserve Releases, Rate-Trend Lag & Cyber Credit Losses

web_blocks.html: While Q3 2026 MCR improved 150 bps YoY to 88.4% and 9M 2026 MCR improved 180 bps YoY to 86.3%, Q3 2026 Form 10-Q Notes 1 and 4 reveal three underlying unit-economics frictions that temper headline margin recovery [29]. First, 9M 2026 reported medical costs ($225,829 million vs $227,600 million current-year incurred) benefited from $1,440 million of favorable prior-years' medical cost reserve development (versus $30 million in 9M 2025) plus $331 million in net reductions to premium deficiency and loss-contract reserves (versus a $250 million reserve build in 9M 2025)—a combined $1.77 billion (~68 bps of 9M 2026 premiums) tailwind that will not recur indefinitely [29]. IBNR reserves stood at $26.7 billion at both December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026 [29].

Second, Q3 2026 MD&A explicitly warns that even the finalized +2.48% CY2027 CMS Medicare Advantage rate notice remains below expected industry forward medical cost trend, compounding multi-year MA rate shortfalls [29]. In commercial plans, medical cost trend remains elevated due to No Surprises Act independent dispute resolution (IDR) outcomes and more aggressive provider service bundling, while Medicaid state rate updates continue to lag behavioral, pharmacy, and home-health acuity [29]. Third, UHC's commitment to cut total prior authorizations by 30% and eliminate >2,000 pediatric CPT codes effective December 1, 2026 reduces regulatory friction but removes a historical utilization brake [30]. Separately, Change Healthcare remediation extended beyond 2024's $2.87 billion impact: in Q4 2025, UNH recorded an additional $799 million credit-loss reserve on provider loans and customer balances within Optum Insight [2].

book_paragraphs: To see how UnitedHealth Group actually makes money—and why it throws off tens of billions in cash even in a bruised year like 2025—we need to strip away the healthcare jargon. Let's follow a single hundred-dollar bill through the machine. Healthcare is often described as overwhelmingly complex, and clinically it is. Economically, however, UNH's unit economics come down to a tight spread between premium pricing, medical claims, drug procurement, and administrative efficiency.

Start with distribution. UNH doesn't wait for patients to walk into a storefront. On the commercial side, it sells through benefit consultants like Mercer and Aon to Fortune 500 human-resources departments. Those multi-year administrative relationships are sticky because switching insurers disrupts every employee's doctor network. In Medicare, UNH pairs its AARP brand partnership with armies of independent brokers during the seven-week fall enrollment window. In Medicaid, it bids directly on multi-year state government RFPs. Once a member enters the funnel, Optum's clinical, pharmacy, and payment engines go to work.

Now look at the FY2025 audited waterfall for every $100 of revenue that entered the door. Out of $447.6 billion in total revenue, $81.47 per hundred—or $364.7 billion—went straight back out to pay doctors, hospitals, and drugmakers. Another $13.31 covered operating costs, payroll, technology, and restructuring, while $0.97 went to depreciation and amortization. That left just $4.24 per hundred in operating profit, down sharply from $8.07 in 2024. In a capital-intensive manufacturing business, a 4.2% operating margin would trigger a five-alarm cash crisis.

Yet UNH still generated $19.7 billion in operating cash flow and $16.1 billion in free cash flow in 2025. That equals roughly $3.59 of free cash for every $100 of revenue. How does a 4.2% margin business produce 154% net-income-to-cash conversion? Two reasons stand out. First, UNH is remarkably asset-light on physical capital. Capital expenditures for property, equipment, and capitalized software were only $3.62 billion, or 0.8% of revenue. Second, insurance runs on negative working capital. UNH collects premiums on the first of the month and holds $39.4 billion in medical-costs-payable float for an average of 47 days before claims are paid. Meanwhile, it earns investment income on an $86.6 billion cash and bond portfolio.

The real risk in UNH's unit economics is not capital intensity; it is pricing lag. Medicare Advantage bids are submitted in June for the following calendar year. Because of that calendar, a sudden spike in outpatient surgeries or drug costs cannot be repriced for twelve to eighteen months. That exact lag caught UNH in 2025. In 2026, management is deliberately shrinking unprofitable risk contracts, cutting prior authorizations by 30%, and shifting Optum Rx to transparent per-member fees. Together, those moves are restoring consolidated operating margins back toward 7% in the first nine months of 2026.

You also need to see how that pricing lag hits Optum Health's value-based care clinics. When Optum Health signs a full-risk capitation contract, it agrees to manage a senior's entire medical budget for a fixed share of the CMS premium. In a benign utilization year, preventive care keeps patients out of the hospital and Optum pockets the savings. In 2025, however, CMS's V28 coding model cut risk-adjusted revenue per patient just as hospital outpatient and specialist use jumped. Because Optum Health carries fixed clinic payroll and physician salaries, it suffered sharp negative operating leverage. The unit swung from $7.8 billion in operating profit to a $278 million loss. Exiting 700,000 patients in sub-scale markets and repricing third-party contracts in 2026 has already pulled Optum Health back to a 4.3% operating margin. That rebound proves the model works when local density and contract pricing match medical acuity.

A forensic reading of the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q also exposes three hidden frictions beneath UNH's recovering margins. First, 9M 2026 reported medical costs benefited from $1.44 billion in favorable prior-year reserve development plus $331 million in loss-contract reserve releases—a $1.77 billion non-recurring cushion worth roughly 68 basis points on the medical care ratio. Second, management explicitly cautions in its 10-Q that even the +2.48% Medicare Advantage payment increase for 2027 trails expected medical cost inflation, while No Surprises Act arbitration disputes keep commercial unit costs elevated and state Medicaid rates lag behavioral and pharmacy acuity. Third, Change Healthcare's financial tail extended into late 2025 via an incremental $799 million credit reserve on care-provider loans, even as UHC eliminates over 2,000 pediatric prior-authorization codes in December 2026 to repair provider trust.

book_callouts.text: Even when underwriting margins compress, UNH's $39.4 billion medical-claims-payable float and 0.8% CapEx-to-revenue ratio allow it to convert earnings into free cash flow at >100% efficiency over a full cycle.
